read.sections.0.text.source: AI tools that write, answer questions or translate learn from training data. For them, it is a huge amount of writing, much of it from the internet. People speak thousands of languages, but most big AI tools learned mainly from English. A low-resource language has little digital material that computers can use for a task. This might be writing, recordings or word lists. The name is about data, not about the language or its speakers. About 200 million people speak Swahili, but there is not enough Swahili writing online for AI to learn well. In Harbourside, Language C is like this.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI tools that write, answer questions or translate learn from training data. For those tools, training data is a very large amount of writing, much of which comes from the internet. People speak thousands of languages, but most big AI tools learned mainly from English. A low-resource language is a language that has only a little digital material that computers can use for a task. This material can be writing, recordings or word lists. This name is about data, not about the language or its speakers. About 200 million people speak Swahili, but there is not enough writing in Swahili on the internet for AI to learn well. In Harbourside, Language C is like this.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Low-resource language" as "bahasa bersumber daya rendah", the term Indonesian language-technology writing uses; the reading and glossary explain it is about data, as the English does.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: Tools that write, answer or translate learn from training data. This is lots of writing from the web. Most big AI tools learned from English. Some languages have little writing or speech for computers. We call this a low-resource language. The name is about data. It is not about the language or the people. About 200 million people speak Swahili. But there is not much written in it online.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: Tools that write, answer or translate learn from training data. This training data is lots of writing from the internet. Most big AI tools learned from English. Some languages have only a little writing or recording for computers. We call this a low-resource language. This name is about data. This name is not about the language or its people. About 200 million people speak Swahili. But there is not much writing in that language on the internet.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Who gets left out, and why
read.sections.1.heading.back: Who gets left behind, and why

read.sections.1.text.source: When a tool works badly in a language, its speakers get worse help. How much writing a language has online is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools and offices mostly use Languages A and B. So little is written in Language C. Masakhane is a group of African researchers. It says African languages have a small place in tech partly because of colonialism. That was when other countries ruled much of Africa. The people who build AI tools also choose which languages to include.
read.sections.1.text.back: When a tool works badly in a language, its speakers get worse help. How much writing a language has on the internet is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools and offices mostly use Languages A and B. So only a little is written in Language C. Masakhane is a group of African researchers. This group says that African languages have only a small place in technology, partly because of colonialism. That was the time when other countries ruled most of Africa. The people who make AI tools also choose which languages are included.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Colonialism" as "penjajahan", the everyday Indonesian word, which Indonesian learners know from their own history; "kolonialisme" is the formal word. Keep this short (sensitive notes).

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A tool can work badly in a language. Then its speakers get worse help. This is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools use Languages A and B. Some African experts say the past matters too. Other countries once ruled much of Africa. That is one reason their languages are left out. AI builders choose which languages to use.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A tool can work badly in a language. Then people who use that language get worse help. This is linked to history and power. In Harbourside, schools use Languages A and B. Some experts from Africa say that the past matters too. In the past other countries ruled most of Africa. That is one reason their languages are left behind. AI makers choose which languages are used.

read.sections.2.heading.source: People build tools for their own languages
read.sections.2.heading.back: People make tools for their own languages

read.sections.2.text.source: Now many people are building tools for their own languages. In Singapore, a programme paid for by the government, AI Singapore, builds models called SEA-LION. A 2025 paper by its team says they support 11 languages used in the region, including Burmese, Khmer, Tamil and Vietnamese. But learning from a language is not the same as working well in it. The team's main tests covered only four of those languages. In Jakarta in November 2024, two companies launched Sahabat-AI for Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and Sundanese. Its makers said it beat similar models, but was at an early stage. Masakhane's name means “We build together” in isiZulu. Its members build tools for African languages, with the people who speak them. Speakers can help a tool fit their community, but people still need to test it.
read.sections.2.text.back: Now many people are making tools for their own languages. In Singapore, a programme paid for by the government, AI Singapore, makes models called SEA-LION. A 2025 paper from its team says that those models support 11 languages used in this region, including Burmese, Khmer, Tamil and Vietnamese. But learning from a language is not the same as working well in that language. That team's main test only covered four of those languages. In Jakarta in November 2024, two companies launched Sahabat-AI for Indonesian, Javanese and Sundanese. Its makers said the model beat similar models, but was still at an early stage. The name Masakhane means “We build together” in isiZulu. Its members make tools for African languages, together with the people who speak them. Speakers can help a tool fit their community, but people still need to test it.
read.sections.2.text.note: Sahabat-AI was launched in Jakarta for Indonesian, Javanese and Sundanese, so it is close to home for the pilot; the teachers' note asks that learners never need to name a language they speak.

watch.summary.source: This video asks why AI tools work better in some languages than in others. A tool like a chatbot learns by reading lots of writing. The video says it is like a giant bookshop. But the bookshop has a problem. Most of its books are in English and a few other big languages. Languages with little writing online are called low-resource languages. The tools know much less about them. The video looks at two of these, Jamaican Patois and Catalan. It also shows researchers who built an open model in many languages, with help from local communities. The presenter says a few big companies decide what goes into these tools. He says it matters to everyone that AI tools include many languages.

The video looks at two of them, Jamaican Patois and Catalan. The video also shows researchers who made an open model in many languages, with help from local communities. educatorNotes.0.source: The Harbourside results (19, 15 and 6 of 20) are made up. The real facts, with their scope: Stanford HAI (2025) defines low-resource languages as those with limited computer-readable data, and gives Swahili (about 200 million speakers) as an example; “low-resource” is about the data for a task (writing, recordings, labelled examples), never about a language's worth or its speakers' skill, and a language can be low-resource for one task and not another. SEA-LION: the 2025 paper (arXiv 2504.05747, version 4, October 2025) describes Llama-SEA-LION-8B-IT and Gemma-SEA-LION-9B-IT, built by AI Singapore with NUS and funded by Singapore's National Research Foundation; the family supports 11 languages (English, Chinese, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Malay, Thai, Burmese, Lao, Filipino, Tamil and Khmer). Supporting a language in training is not proof that it works well: the paper's main benchmark (SEA-HELM) tested only Indonesian, Vietnamese, Thai and Tamil, and a wider test (SEACrowd) covered 31 regional languages but only classic language tasks, not chat; the authors list this as a limitation. The first SEA-LION model (Context, February 2024) was trained on text that was about 63% English, and critics warned that regional models can repeat the views of powerful groups. Sahabat-AI: GoTo's press release (15 November 2024) says it was co-developed with Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, launched with 8- and 9-billion-parameter models for Bahasa Indonesia, Javanese and Sundanese (Batak and Balinese planned), is open source, and “demonstrated leading performance” against similar open models; that is the makers' claim, with no published scores in the release, and it calls the project early. Masakhane's own description links the small place of African languages in technology partly to colonialism. Older learners could discuss who owns these tools and who tests them.
educatorNotes.0.back: The results in Harbourside (19, 15 and 6 of 20) are made up. SEA-LION: the 2025 paper (arXiv 2504.05747, version 4, October 2025) describes Llama-SEA-LION-8B-IT and Gemma-SEA-LION-9B-IT, made by AI Singapore with NUS and funded by Singapore's National Research Foundation; this model family supports 11 languages (English, Chinese, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Malay, Thai, Burmese, Lao, Filipino, Tamil and Khmer). Supporting a language in training is not proof that the model works well in that language: the paper's main benchmark (SEA-HELM) tested only Indonesian, Vietnamese, Thai and Tamil, and a wider test (SEACrowd) covered 31 languages in this region but only classic language tasks, not conversation; its authors list this as a limitation. The first SEA-LION model (Context, February 2024) was trained on text that was about 63% English, and critics warned that regional models can repeat the views of powerful groups. Sahabat-AI: GoTo's press release (15 November 2024) says that this model was developed together with Indosat Ooredoo Hutchison, launched with models of 8 and 9 billion parameters for Indonesian, Javanese and Sundanese (Batak and Balinese planned), is open source, and “demonstrated leading performance” compared with similar open models; that is its makers' claim, without scores published in that press release, and that press release calls the project still early. Masakhane's own description links the small place of African languages in technology partly to colonialism. Older learners could discuss who owns these tools and who tests them.
